identifier: HoneyGPT: Breaking the Trilemma in Honeypots with Large Language Models
domain_justification: Page 1: The work focuses on "Terminal honeypots," which are "a specialized type of honeypots for emulating real terminal systems"
interaction_justification: HoneyGPT is a programmatic emulator that "repurposes the work of the Cowrie honeypot" for its protocol proxy". While it uses LLMs to simulate high-interaction results, the authors explicitly baseline it against Cowrie, which they define as a "medium-interaction" system
threat_model: Human attackers engaging in dialogue and commands
threat_model_justification: Page 4: The system is designed for "Adversarial scenarios often involve attackers executing a series of malicious commands" and  Abstract: "bait unauthorized entities"
irb_justification: There is no mention of an "Institutional Review Board," "ethics committee," or "human subject protocols" in the entire paper.
consent_justification: Page 2: The authors explicitly "deploy HoneyGPT... on the Internet for three months" to engage with live attackers, capturing "more attack behaviors and longer interactions" without any mention of obtaining consent
data_types_collected: Conversational data, commands, attacker responses
data_types_justification: Page 3: The Terminal Protocol Proxy "parses attackers’ commands" while the Prompt Manager "extracts the terminal output" and "maintaining the state of honeypot"
protocols_justification: Section IV: The system uses a "Terminal Protocol Proxy" that "repurposes the work of the Cowrie honeypot" to parse attacker commands (Cowrie typically handles ports 22/23)
data_sensitivity_justification: Page 2: The system maintains "dynamic memory during interactions" and "long-dialogue response tasks," which involve high-fidelity logs of human-adversary interactions
data_minimization_justification: Page4: No mention of the "minimization principle"; the focus is instead on "Memory Pruning" to handle context length limits for better interaction
data_retention_justification: Page 5: "Memory Maintenance" is discussed strictly in the context of "managing the prompt’s length" rather than a formal retention or deletion policy for stored interaction logs
data_sharing_justification: Page 2: While "baseline evaluation" and P1: "field evaluation" results are discussed, there is no mention of a public link to the interaction traces or conversational datasets
jurisdiction_justification: Page 2: The paper mentions deployment "on the Internet for three months" but contains no analysis of "GDPR," "legal compliance," or jurisdictional awareness
containment_justification: Page3: The framework "transforms the conventional ”requestresponse” message interaction (based on terminal protocols) into a ”question-answer” text interaction (via ChatGPT API)" effectively isolating the attacker's impact within the LLM's simulated environment
deception_justification: Page 6: Deception is central to the design, aiming to "expertly balances authenticity with the objective of enticing attackers into prolonged interactions"
researcher_responsibility_justification: The authors discuss  Page9: "security analysis features" and a P10: "paradigm shift" for threat intelligence, but do not provide a formal ethical responsibility statement
ethical_gaps: Major ethical concerns (manipulation, consent, AI agency) not addressed
ethical_gaps_justification: Page 11: The paper acknowledges technical "limitations" such as "Prompt-based Attacks" and "Overfitting," but ignores the human-centric ethical risks of AI-driven manipulation and the lack of informed consent
relevance_to_project: Critical case study for ethical risks of LLM honeypots
relevance_justification: Critical case study for the "technology-driven ethical lag" and the "structural ethical vacuum." While HoneyGPT solves the technical "trilemma" using LLMs to create a high-fidelity digital twin of a terminal , it lacks the IRB oversight and ethical governance found in HoneySat . It serves as the primary example of why a new Ethical Framework is mandatory for AI-driven systems that interact with humans in the wild without consent .
deployment_justification: Page 2: "We deploy HoneyGPT and Cowire, which is a programmatic honeypot, on the Internet for three months"

identifier: A High-interaction Physics-aware ICS Honeypot for Industrial Environments

identifier: Liebergeld, S., Lange, M., & Borgaonkar, R. (2014). Cellpot: A Concept for Next Generation Cellular Network Honeypots. SENT Workshop, NDSS 2014.
domain_justification: The paper proposes Cellpot, a novel honeypot concept deployed directly inside the cellular network on small cell (femtocell) base stations to detect and mitigate signaling attacks, SMS spam, and mobile malware. It is explicitly and specifically a honeypot design paper.
interaction_justification: Cellpot is a low-interaction honeypot: it performs anomaly detection and traffic monitoring on signaling data, it does not allow full attacker control or deep interaction with core network functions.
threat_model: Mobile network attackers using compromised smartphones to execute signaling DoS attacks, SMS spam, and mobile malware propagation against the cellular core network.
threat_model_justification: Section III (Threat Model): "we assume an attacker who has physical access to a femto- or small cell base station...The attackers possess one or more mobile devices which enables them to connect to the base station and create signaling traffic."
irb_justification: No section in the paper mentions IRB, ethics committee, institutional approval, or human subjects protocol. The paper is purely a technical/conceptual design.
consent_justification: The paper does not discuss consent, attacker notification, or any form of disclosure. Concept paper with no mention of consent model.
data_types_collected: Signaling traffic, IMSI numbers, call history, SMS content, browsing history (conceptual)
data_types_justification: Section V (Discussion: Legal Issues): "data collected by Cellpot can contain user's private information such as International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) number, call history, and even the browsing history etc."
protocols_ports: SS7 signaling, IPSec VPN (TR-069), cellular radio (2G/3G/LTE)
protocols_justification: Section II and IV: Femtocell communicates via IPSec VPN through SeGW to core network. Monitors SS7 signaling channels and radio interface.
data_sensitivity_justification: Section V: The system can capture IMSI numbers, call history, SMS content, and browsing history highly sensitive personal identifiers. Paper acknowledges "private nature of this data could raise privacy concerns."
data_minimization_justification: No mention of data minimization, anonymization, or selective logging in any section of the paper.
data_retention_justification: No retention policy or deletion timeline mentioned anywhere in the paper.
data_sharing_justification: No dataset release, no public traces, no mention of data sharing with third parties beyond MNO.
jurisdiction_justification: Section V (Discussion): "The private nature of this data could raise privacy concerns in some countries." Authors note MNOs already provide lawful interception interfaces and store data per local laws, arguing Cellpot will not create legal issues but no detailed jurisdiction analysis.
containment_measures: Architectural isolation of firmware and infrastructure environments; P2P network with master node control; IPSec encryption of core network communications.
containment_justification: Section VI: Proposes partitioning femtocell into isolated Firmware Environment (FE) and Infrastructure Environment (IE) using a microkernel. "By isolating both environments we assure that rooted firmware can be controlled."
deception_justification: The paper discusses deception only in technical terms (small cells "act like honeypots" because their stronger signal lures devices). No ethical framing of deception is provided.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No statements about researcher responsibility, ethical guidelines, responsible disclosure, or dual-use considerations appear in the paper.
ethical_gaps: High privacy risk (IMSI/call/browsing data captured); no IRB; no consent model; no data governance; conceptual only, not tested, so harm is theoretical but design enables mass surveillance.
ethical_gaps_justification: Section V: Authors acknowledge sensitivity of IMSI, call history, and browsing data but dismiss legal concern by citing existing MNO lawful interception practices. No anonymization scheme proposed despite acknowledging "certified anonymizing algorithms" are necessary.
relevance_to_project: Relevant to HoneySat/Ethics framework: demonstrates honeypot deployment in critical infrastructure (cellular network) with high-sensitivity personal data capture strong case study for ethical risk framework covering data governance and legal compliance in honeypots.
relevance_justification: Cellpot is designed for deployment inside live cellular networks capturing real user signaling data, directly analogous to HoneySat operating within critical infrastructure. The absence of IRB and data governance mirrors gaps our ethics framework aims to address.
deployment_justification: Paper explicitly states this is a "novel concept" and "practical software design." No deployment or experimental evaluation is described. The concept targets deployment inside live MNO cellular networks but no live deployment is reported.

identifier: Guan, C., & Cao, G. (2025). Cyber-Physical Deception Through Coordinated IoT Honeypots. 34th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 25), pp. 529–545.
domain_justification: The paper proposes a Cyber-Physical Deception System (CPDS) that coordinates multiple IoT honeypots to mimic cyber-physical dependencies among IoT devices, making honeypots undetectable by cross-layer attackers. It is explicitly a honeypot design and deployment paper for IoT/CPS environments.
interaction_justification: CPDS coordinates multiple honeypots with modeled vulnerabilities and physical/network dependency rules. Attackers can interact with services and receive consistent cross-layer responses  higher than low-interaction but not full system access, making this medium interaction.
threat_model: IoT device attackers operating across both cyber (network exploitation) and physical (device state verification) domains, capable of detecting inconsistencies among honeypots through multi-source attacks.
threat_model_justification: Abstract: "attackers can easily detect inconsistencies among the honeypots after launching attacks from multiple sources, spanning both cyber and physical domains, to verify device status."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, institutional approval, or human subjects protocol in any section of the paper.
consent_justification: Honeypots are deployed facing real-world attackers. No consent or disclosure mechanism is described. Attackers are treated implicitly as adversaries whose interactions are logged without notification.
data_types_collected: Attack traces, attacker IP addresses, CVE exploit attempts, device interaction logs, physical state queries
data_types_justification: Paper describes collecting and analyzing "attack traces" to model device vulnerabilities. CVE identifiers (CVE-2020-12109, CVE-2021-44402, CVE-2018-3928, CVE-2019-3949, CVE-2020-35577) are referenced as attack data collected.
protocols_ports: UPnP, device-specific IoT protocols; ports vary by emulated device (smart plug, smart bulb, router, camera)
protocols_justification: Related work section references U-POT (UPnP protocol), and the system emulates protocol-level responses for various IoT device types. Specific ports depend on emulated device class.
data_sensitivity_justification: Data includes attacker IPs and CVE-specific exploit traces. No personal benign user data is described. Medium sensitivity given identifiable attacker network metadata and potential cross-domain device state information.
data_minimization_justification: No mention of data minimization, IP anonymization, or selective logging in any section.
data_retention_justification: No data retention policy, deletion timeline, or archival policy mentioned in the paper.
data_sharing_justification: No dataset release or public trace sharing is described in the paper.
jurisdiction_justification: No jurisdiction analysis, GDPR compliance discussion, or legal framing appears in any section of the paper despite deployment facing real-world IoT attackers.
containment_measures: Honeypot isolation implied; physical process emulated synthetically (no real IoT devices attached to physical processes); Prolog rule-based dependency enforcement ensures consistent fake state.
containment_justification: The system models physical dependencies as Prolog rules and coordinates honeypot responses to ensure cross-layer consistency real physical processes are not connected, preventing actual harm. Containment is technical by design.
deception_justification: Deception is discussed entirely as a technical coordination problem ("cross-layer consistency," "cyber-physical dependency emulation"). No ethical framing of deception, attacker engagement, or dual-use considerations appears.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility statements, ethical guidelines, or responsible disclosure discussion appear anywhere in the paper.
ethical_gaps: No IRB; no consent model; no data governance; no legal/jurisdiction discussion despite real-world deployment. Dual-use risk of coordinated deception infrastructure not acknowledged.
ethical_gaps_justification: No ethics section exists. Despite deployment facing real-world IoT attackers with logging of attacker IPs and CVE exploit attempts, there is no discussion of data protection, responsible disclosure, or regulatory compliance.
relevance_to_project: Highly relevant to HoneySat/Ethics framework and Digital Twin: directly addresses cyber-physical honeypot coordination in IoT/CPS environments, the closest parallel to satellite/space CPS honeypot design. Demonstrates need for ethical framework governing multi-layer deception in CPS contexts.
relevance_justification: CPDS addresses precisely the problem HoneySat faces: maintaining cross-layer consistency in a cyber-physical honeypot to prevent detection. The absence of ethical governance mirrors the gap our framework targets. Published at USENIX Security 2025 high-impact, recent, directly relevant.
deployment_justification: The system is designed to face real-world IoT attackers and collects actual attack traces and CVE exploit data. The paper describes deployment against real attacker traffic, not just controlled lab evaluation.

identifier: Sladić, M., Valeros, V., Catania, C., & Garcia, S. (2023). LLM in the Shell: Generative Honeypots. ESORICS 2023 Poster Session, The Hague, Netherlands. IEEE. arXiv:2309.00155.
domain_justification: Abstract: "This work introduces shelLM, a dynamic and realistic software honeypot based on Large Language Models that generates Linux-like shell output." The paper explicitly proposes, implements, and evaluates a new honeypot named shelLM. The paper is in the "Honeypots" category of cybersecurity research.
interaction_justification: The shelLM honeypot allows real interactive SSH sessions where human attackers execute actual Linux commands and receive dynamic LLM-generated responses. This is above low-interaction (which only emulates services) but not full high-interaction (no real OS access). Evaluation section: "12 human participants tested shelLM" and "Participants executed 226 commands associated with package management, file system management, network operations, system information, and file management."
threat_model: Human attackers capable of distinguishing real Linux shell from a fake one; SSH brute-force attackers and skilled human penetration testers who can fingerprint traditional honeypots.
threat_model_justification: Abstract: "most of them lack the required realism to engage and fool human attackers long-term." Evaluation: "We evaluated the realism of each command by conducting an experiment with human attackers who needed to say if the answer from the honeypot was fake or not."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval anywhere in the paper. The paper is entirely technically framed.
consent_justification: The evaluation uses cybersecurity researchers as human participants who knowingly interact with the honeypot. Abstract: "The evaluation was done by asking cybersecurity researchers to use the honeypot and give feedback." This implies informed participation in the evaluation. However, real-world attacker consent is not discussed.
data_types_collected: SSH session commands, shell interaction logs, command outputs, attacker behaviour during evaluation
data_types_justification: Evaluation section: "Participants executed 226 commands associated with package management, file system management, network operations, system information, and file management." The system logs all commands and responses through the SSH session.
protocols_justification: Paper describes: "SSH to allow secure access by the participants." The honeypot runs as an SSH server, so all interaction is over SSH port 22.
data_sensitivity_justification: The evaluation uses cybersecurity researchers in a controlled study, and no personal user data is collected. The commands logged are shell commands (ls, ping, wget, etc.) which carry low sensitivity. No identifiable attacker data from real-world deployment is described.
data_minimization_justification: No discussion of data minimization, log retention, or privacy filtering of the evaluation session data.
data_retention_justification: No data retention policy or storage timeline mentioned in any section of the paper.
data_sharing: Source code and prompts released publicly
data_sharing_justification: arXiv abstract: "The source code and prompts for replicating the experiments have been publicly available." The shelLM code is open source, enabling replication. No raw session log dataset is released.
jurisdiction_justification: No jurisdiction analysis, privacy law compliance, or legal framework is discussed despite the system using OpenAI API (cloud-based data processing) for generating responses.
containment_measures: Controlled evaluation with consenting cybersecurity researchers; no real attacker deployment described in this paper
containment_justification: Evaluation section: "Each participant was randomly assigned a unique honeypot instance." The evaluation is structured as a controlled user study, not a live internet deployment. The honeypot is isolated per participant and session-based.
deception_justification: The entire paper is technically framed. Deception is discussed only as a design goal: Abstract: "most of them lack the required realism to engage and fool human attackers long-term." No ethical dimension of using deception on real attackers is discussed.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility statements, ethical guidelines, responsible disclosure, or dual-use discussion appear in the paper.
ethical_gaps: Uses cloud-based OpenAI API (GPT-3.5-turbo-16k), all shell interaction data is sent to a third-party API, raising data privacy concerns not addressed. No ethics section. No IRB. No discussion of potential misuse (an attacker could use the same LLM shell spoofing against defenders). No privacy policy for session data.
ethical_gaps_justification: Paper section on system design: "OpenAI API for GPT-3.5-turbo-16k." Every attacker command and honeypot response is transmitted to OpenAI's cloud API, creating a third-party data processing relationship. No discussion of GDPR compliance, data processing agreements, or privacy implications of sending potentially sensitive attacker interaction data to a commercial API.
relevance_to_project: Highly relevant to HoneySat and Ethics framework: demonstrates LLM-based adaptive honeypot design which is directly applicable to space/satellite honeypot scenarios requiring dynamic, realistic responses. The OpenAI API dependency and the absence of any data governance framework make this a key case study in the need for ethical guidelines for AI-powered honeypots.
relevance_justification: The shelLM design using LLMs to generate credible, adaptive responses to attackers  directly parallels approaches being considered for HoneySat to deceive sophisticated nation-state attackers. The complete absence of ethics discussion despite using third-party cloud AI for processing attacker interactions reinforces the gap our framework addresses.
deployment: Controlled evaluation only (not deployed in the wild)
deployment_justification: The paper describes a controlled user study with 12 cybersecurity researcher participants. Evaluation section: "Each participant was randomly assigned a unique honeypot instance." No live internet-facing deployment is reported in this paper. The shelLM system uses SSH for the evaluation but no public IP exposure or real attacker capture is described.

identifier: Valeros, V., Rigaki, M., & Garcia, S. (2023). Attacker Profiling Through Analysis of Attack Patterns in Geographically Distributed Honeypots. arXiv:2305.01346. Czech Technical University, Prague.
domain_justification: Abstract: "This paper examines attack patterns in a large public dataset of geographically distributed honeypots by answering methodological questions and creating behavioural profiles of attackers." The paper deploys 8 real honeypots across 8 global cities (Amsterdam, Bangalore, Frankfurt, London, New York, San Francisco, Singapore, Toronto) for 40 days and uses the CTU Hornet 40 dataset created by the authors. This is an actual honeypot deployment and analysis paper.
interaction_justification: Section 3 (Dataset): "Each Linux-based VPS was configured to act as a passive honeypot without any service, receiving attacks without running any honeypot software." The honeypots are passive, they receive and log network traffic without any simulated services or interaction with attackers. This is lower than low-interaction as there is no service emulation.
threat_model: All types of real-world internet attackers: automated bots, IoT botnets, brute-force scripts, and targeted human attackers. Section 5.5 defines four profiles: Casual Focused (73.26%), Casual Explorer (2.7%), Driven Focused (15.74%), and Driven Explorer (8.3%).
threat_model_justification: Section 5.1: "54.87% of the total attackers originate from Asia, 16.84% from Europe, and 15.01% from North America." Section 5.5: "Of the total attacker, 8.3% can be profiled as driven explorer attackers...responsible for 37.4% of the total attacks."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval anywhere in the paper. The paper is framed as a measurement and analysis study using existing public data.
consent_justification: The honeypots are passive network sensors. No services are offered, no interaction occurs, and there is no mechanism for consent or notification. Attackers are implicitly treated as adversaries whose traffic is logged without any disclosure.
data_types_collected: Attacker IP addresses, network flows (bidirectional), destination ports, attack timestamps, geographic origin, Tor exit node membership
data_types_justification: Section 3 (Dataset): "The dataset contains 4,747,081 attacks, performed by 265,423 unique attackers, to 8 geographically-distributed honeypots, during 40 days." Section 4: "Attack: an attack is defined as a network flow whose destination IP address matches one of the IPs of the honeypots. Attacker: an attacker is defined as the source IP address in an attack."
protocols_ports: All TCP and UDP ports (passive capture, no specific ports opened)
protocols_justification: Section 3: "Each Linux-based VPS was configured to act as a passive honeypot without any service." Section 4.3: "This question refers to services of the TCP and UDP protocols since other protocols do not have services." The honeypots capture all incoming traffic on any port.
data_sensitivity_justification: Section 4.1.1 acknowledges that "the IP address of a country may not be related to the country itself" and discusses proxies and Tor. IP addresses are collected and analysed as attacker identifiers, these are personal data under GDPR. No anonymization is described. Medium sensitivity: no credentials or commands collected (passive honeypot), but 265,423 unique attacker IPs are logged.
data_minimization_justification: No discussion of data minimization, IP anonymization, or filtering. All network flow data including source IPs is retained and analysed.
data_retention_justification: No data retention policy or deletion timeline mentioned. The dataset (CTU Hornet 40) was published publicly: Reference [28]: "Veronica Valeros and Sebastian Garcia. Hornet 40: Network dataset of geographically placed honeypots. Data in Brief, 40:107795, 2022."
data_sharing_justification: Section 3 references [28]: "CTU Hornet 40 dataset." The dataset containing 4.7M attacks and 265K unique attacker IPs was published in Data in Brief journal and is publicly available. No mention of anonymization before release.
jurisdiction_justification: No jurisdiction analysis, GDPR compliance discussion, or legal framework mentioned despite collecting and publicly releasing IP address data for 265,423 individuals (attackers) across multiple continents and jurisdictions (Section 5.1: Amsterdam, Bangalore, Frankfurt, London, New York, San Francisco, Singapore, Toronto).
containment_measures: Passive monitoring only; VPS isolation in cloud provider infrastructure; no active services to cause collateral harm
containment_justification: Section 3: "Eight Virtual Private Servers (VPS) were rented in the same VPS provider. Each Linux-based VPS was configured to act as a passive honeypot without any service." The passive nature limits harm potential since no interactions occur. VPS cloud isolation provides technical containment.
deception_justification: The paper is entirely a measurement and analysis study. The concept of deception is not discussed, the honeypots are passive sensors, and the paper focuses on statistical profiles of attackers rather than deception design.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility statements, ethical guidelines, or data governance discussion appear. The acknowledgements mention Czech Republic government funding but no ethics committee oversight.
ethical_gaps: Public release of 265,423 attacker IP addresses without anonymization may violate GDPR (IP addresses are personal data in the EU). No IRB. No consent model. No legal analysis despite multi-jurisdictional deployment and data collection. Dataset published openly in Data in Brief.
ethical_gaps_justification: Section 3 and Reference [28]: The CTU Hornet 40 dataset including source IP addresses of attackers was published in a peer-reviewed journal. Given that honeypots were deployed in Amsterdam and Frankfurt (EU jurisdictions), collecting and publishing attacker IP addresses without anonymization may constitute personal data processing under GDPR Art. 4(1). No legal compliance discussion appears in the paper.
relevance_to_project: Highly relevant to HoneySat and Ethics framework: demonstrates multi-geography distributed honeypot deployment with quantitative attacker profiling, directly applicable to satellite ground station honeypot network design. The public dataset release without IP anonymization is a critical ethical case study for data governance frameworks in honeypot research.
relevance_justification: Section 9 (Conclusions): "Analysis indicates that as few as two distributed honeypots can be useful in helping organisations identify the most aggressive and driven attackers." This finding is directly applicable to HoneySat architecture decisions. The absence of any GDPR or legal compliance discussion despite EU-based deployments and public IP release directly motivates the legal pillar of our ethics framework.
deployment: Yes (8 geographically distributed public internet deployments)
deployment_justification: Section 3: "Eight Virtual Private Servers (VPS) were rented in the same VPS provider [DigitalOcean]...in eight cities: Amsterdam, Bangalore, Frankfurt, London, New York, San Francisco, Singapore, and Toronto." The honeypots were deployed on public internet-facing VPS servers for 40 days (April 23 to June 1, 2021), collecting 4.7M real attacks from 265K unique IPs.

identifier: Erquiaga, M. J., & Garcia, S. (2019). Hack Me-Do: Deploying an IoT Malware Laboratory to Analyze Malicious Behavior. Stratosphere Laboratory, Czech Technical University, Prague.
domain_justification: The paper deploys real IoT devices (IP cameras, routers) as honeypots  referred to as an "IoT Malware Laboratory"  exposed to the internet to capture malware infections and analyze malicious behavior. The paper explicitly uses physical IoT devices as high-interaction honeypots and reports real malware capture results. This is an actual honeypot deployment paper targeting IoT/CPS attack surface.
interaction_justification: The deployment uses real physical IoT devices (actual IP cameras and routers) exposed to the internet. These devices run real firmware and operating systems, allowing full interaction with malware. This is a high-interaction setup: attackers interact with the real device OS, can download malware, and execute commands on the real hardware.
threat_model: IoT malware (botnets such as Mirai variants), automated scanners targeting IoT vulnerabilities, and script-based attackers exploiting default credentials on cameras and routers.
threat_model_justification: The paper describes capturing real malware infections on IoT cameras and routers. Attacks include credential brute-force, telnet/SSH exploitation, and malware download commands, all characteristic of IoT botnet recruitment attempts.
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval. The paper describes a technical research deployment with no ethics oversight discussion.
consent_justification: No consent model discussed. Real IoT devices are deployed internet-facing without notification to attackers. Attackers are treated as adversaries whose behavior is logged.
data_types_collected: Network traffic, malware samples, attacker commands, telnet/SSH session logs, device traffic (encrypted and unencrypted), protocol payloads
data_types_justification: The paper captures full network traffic from real IoT devices, including malware download attempts, command-and-control traffic, and post-exploitation commands. Malware samples are collected for analysis.
protocols_ports: Telnet (23), SSH (22), HTTP (80), RTSP (554), device-specific ports (manufacturer dependent)
protocols_justification: Real IoT devices expose the same ports as legitimate devices (Telnet 23, SSH 22, HTTP 80, RTSP 554 for cameras). The entire port surface of the real devices is exposed.
data_sensitivity_justification: Traffic from real IoT devices may include video streams, audio, and device metadata alongside malware interactions. Attacker IPs are logged. Medium sensitivity: primarily malware and botnet traffic, but device traffic characteristics may reveal device location or user patterns.
data_minimization_justification: No data minimization or privacy filtering discussed despite using real physical devices that may capture benign traffic alongside malicious.
data_retention_justification: No retention policy mentioned. The IoT-23 dataset (a product of this research program) was later published publicly.
data_sharing: Malware samples captured; IoT-23 dataset (related) publicly released
data_sharing_justification: The research program led to the IoT-23 dataset, a labeled dataset of IoT malware network traffic  which was publicly released by Stratosphere Laboratory. Malware samples are captured and analyzed.
jurisdiction_justification: No legal or jurisdictional discussion despite deploying internet-facing devices that attract real attackers and capture data from global IP addresses.
containment_measures: Physical device isolation from production network; dedicated research network segment; monitoring and capture of all device traffic
containment_justification: The IoT devices are deployed in a controlled laboratory environment separated from production infrastructure. All traffic is monitored and captured. The physical separation provides containment, the malware infects the isolated device and cannot spread to production systems.
deception_justification: No discussion of deception ethics. The research frames the IoT devices as "bait" to attract malware, which is inherently deceptive, but no ethical analysis of this approach is provided.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility statements or ethical guidelines discussed. No disclosure or responsible disclosure policy mentioned.
ethical_gaps: No IRB; no ethics section; real physical devices expose full attack surface including device-specific vulnerabilities; no discussion of responsibility if a compromised device is used in DDoS attacks against third parties; data governance for captured traffic not addressed.
ethical_gaps_justification: The use of real IoT devices creates a genuine risk: if a device is fully compromised by a botnet, it may be used to attack third parties (DDoS, spam, etc.). This responsibility gap,  the researcher as passive observer of ongoing malicious activity is not discussed in the paper. This is a significant ethical issue for IoT honeypot research.
relevance_to_project: Relevant to HoneySat and Ethics framework: demonstrates high-interaction IoT/CPS honeypot deployment using real physical devices. The risk of compromised devices being weaponized against third parties is a directly applicable concern for satellite/space honeypots where a compromised satellite could cause real harm. This gap in responsibility disclosure motivates the harm prevention pillar of our ethics framework.
relevance_justification: The Stratosphere Lab's IoT malware laboratory  exposing real devices to capture malware represents the most analogous published approach to HoneySat's concept of deploying real (or realistic) space system components as honeypots. The absence of ethical discussion about third-party harm from compromised devices is a critical gap our framework must address.
deployment_justification: Real physical IoT devices (cameras, routers) were deployed with internet-facing connectivity to attract real malware infections. This constitutes a live deployment facing real internet attackers, not a controlled lab evaluation.

identifier: Vasilomanolakis, E., Karuppayah, S., Fischer, M., Plasoianu, M., Pfeiffer, W., Pandikow, L., & Mühlhäuser, M. (2013). This Network is Infected: HosTaGe – a Low-Interaction Honeypot for Mobile Devices. In SPSM@CCS 2013 (pp. 43–48). ACM.
domain_justification: Abstract: "This paper envisions portable honeypots on mobile devices that aim on the fast detection of malicious networks and thus boost the security awareness of users and presents the prototype HosTaGe, a low-interaction honeypot implemented for the Android OS." Explicitly proposes, designs, and implements a new honeypot (HosTaGe) as primary contribution.
interaction_justification: Abstract: "HosTaGe, a low-interaction honeypot implemented for the Android OS." Simulates services (FTP, SSH) at low-interaction level. All incoming connections are considered malicious and logged.
threat_model: Malware and automated attackers propagating through wireless networks; users unknowingly connecting to malicious access points in public spaces (airports, hotels).
threat_model_justification: Introduction: "people tend to utilize unknown, in terms of trustworthiness, wireless networks in their daily life. They connect to these networks, e.g., airports, without knowledge of whether they are safe or infected with actively propagating malware."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval in the paper.
consent_justification: No consent model. The honeypot passively logs all incoming connection attempts on the mobile device. Attackers are treated as adversaries without any notification.
data_types_collected: Incoming connection logs, protocol interaction data, attacker IP addresses, malware propagation attempts
data_types_justification: HosTaGe description: "As any incoming connections are considered malicious, all subsequent communication with HosTaGe is logged, for further analysis." Services emulated include FTP and SSH.
protocols_ports: FTP (21), SSH (22), and other configurable ports on the Android device network interface
protocols_justification: HosTaGe emulates multiple services (FTP, SSH) on standard ports. All standard protocol ports exposed on the device's wireless network interface.
data_sensitivity_justification: Captures incoming network connection attempts on a mobile device. No personal user data beyond attacker IPs and protocol data. Low sensitivity.
data_sharing: Source code released as open-source Android app (GitHub: aau-network-security/HosTaGe)
data_sharing_justification: HosTaGe is released as an open-source Android application available for community download and deployment.
jurisdiction_justification: No legal framework discussion. Published at a 2013 workshop; pre-GDPR era, but no privacy discussion of any kind.
containment_measures: App isolation within Android OS; honeypot runs as separate application without interfering with normal phone functions
containment_justification: The honeypot runs as a standalone Android application. Android OS provides baseline isolation from other apps. The honeypot has no access to personal user data on the device.
deception_justification: No ethical framing of deception. Portable mobile honeypot concept presented purely as a security mechanism without discussing ethical implications of luring attackers on personal devices.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No ethical guidelines, responsible disclosure, or researcher responsibility discussed.
ethical_gaps: No IRB; no ethics section; deploys honeypot on personal mobile devices that may be carried into private spaces, novel privacy risk dimension not addressed; personal device IP and presence exposed to potential attackers.
ethical_gaps_justification: The use of a personal mobile device as a honeypot on unknown wireless networks creates a novel risk: the device owner's network presence is exposed to potential attackers. If attackers scan back or identify the honeypot operator, the personal device may become a target. This user-risk dimension is not addressed.
relevance_to_project: Relevant to HoneySat ethics framework: first mobile honeypot, establishes the research line Vasilomanolakis later extended to IoT/OT environments. The portable honeypot concept directly parallels deploying space-borne honeypots in sensitive environments.
relevance_justification: HosTaGe is the foundational work in this professor's honeypot research line. The absence of any ethical framework for personal device honeypot deployment particularly the risk to the device owner is a gap directly relevant to HoneySat operator safety considerations.
deployment: Yes (deployed on mobile devices in real wireless networks)
deployment_justification: The paper describes real-world deployment of HosTaGe on mobile devices connecting to unknown wireless networks, collecting real attack data from malicious access points.

identifier: Srinivasa, S., Pedersen, J. M., & Vasilomanolakis, E. (2021). RIoTPot: A Modular Hybrid-Interaction IoT/OT Honeypot. In Computer Security – ESORICS 2021 (LNCS Vol. 12973, pp. 745–751). Springer.
domain_justification: Abstract: "In this paper, we introduce RIoTPot, a modular and hybrid-interaction honeypot for Internet-of-Things (IoT) and Operational Technology (OT) protocols mainly used in Industrial Control System environments." Proposes, designs, and deploys a new honeypot as its primary contribution.
interaction_justification: Section 2: explicitly introduces a "hybrid-interaction" model enabling users to "switch between low- and high-interaction modes." Low-interaction via software packages; high-interaction via containers running full protocol implementations. Hybrid model spans both classified as medium overall.
threat_model: Adversaries targeting IoT and OT protocols including Telnet, SSH, CoAP, Modbus, and MQTT. Both automated scanners and sophisticated attackers targeting ICS/SCADA environments.
threat_model_justification: Section 3: "A total of 7,587 attacks were observed across all the protocols simulated by RIoTPot." Section 1: "low-interaction honeypots are prone to fingerprinting attacks due to their limited emulation capabilities."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval.
consent_justification: Section 3: "We define an attack as any interaction with the honeypot as there is no production value whatsoever." All interactions logged without notification. No consent model.
data_types_collected: Attack traffic (pcap via tcpdump), attack counts per protocol per day, attacker IPs, MQTT topic creation/subscription/deletion/modification records
data_types_justification: Section 2: "The attack capture component is responsible for storing the attack packets as pcap files, using tcpdump." Section 3: "recurring sessions from same suspicious actors on the high-interaction mode, that included topic creation, subscription and deletion, and modification of existing messages."
protocols_justification: Section 3: "In the low-interaction variant, the protocols SSH, Telnet, HTTP, MQTT, CoAP and Modbus were simulated through the plug-in packages, while the high-interaction variant simulated the MQTT protocol in a container."
data_sensitivity_justification: Attack traffic includes attacker IP addresses and detailed MQTT interaction records (topic creation, message modification). No personal user data collected; medium sensitivity given identifiable attacker network metadata and ICS protocol interaction logs.
data_minimization_justification: No data minimization. Noise filter removes known scanning engines (Shodan, Censys) but full attacker IPs retained.
data_sharing_justification: Section 2: GitHub link provided. RIoTPot is fully open-source with documentation.
jurisdiction_justification: No legal or jurisdiction analysis despite deploying internet-facing honeypots emulating ICS/OT protocols (Modbus, MQTT, CoAP) used in critical infrastructure.
containment_measures: Noise filter module removes well-known scanning services; database module isolated from honeypot modules; containers provide process isolation for high-interaction mode
containment_justification: Section 2: "The attack database stores all the attack traffic received on the honeypot. The database is setup as an independent module to ensure data availability even if a honeypot module is down." Containers provide process isolation for high-interaction MQTT service.
deception_justification: Deception framed entirely technically. No ethical framing of emulating ICS/SCADA protocols (Modbus used in power plants, water treatment) as a deception mechanism.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility discussion. No acknowledgement of dual-use risks of publishing open-source ICS/OT honeypot designs.
ethical_gaps: No IRB; no ethics section; open-source ICS/OT honeypot emulating Modbus (industrial control) creates dual-use risk attackers can use the code to test their tools against a realistic ICS honeypot before attacking real critical infrastructure.
ethical_gaps_justification: Open-source release of RIoTPot with Modbus, MQTT, and CoAP emulation creates dual-use concern: the same code enabling defenders to collect threat intelligence can help attackers test ICS attack tools against a realistic honeypot before targeting real power plants or water treatment facilities. This is not acknowledged in the paper.
relevance_to_project: Highly relevant to HoneySat ethics framework: RIoTPot directly addresses cyber-physical IoT/OT honeypot design closest published framework to a satellite/space CPS honeypot. The hybrid-interaction model and modular container architecture are directly applicable to HoneySat design.
relevance_justification: Section 4: "as future work, we aim to extend RIoTPot to support more IoT and OT protocols like S7, DNP3, Fieldbus and Profibus." These are nuclear plant and industrial protocols. Open-source ICS honeypot design without ethical governance is precisely the gap HoneySat's framework addresses.
deployment: Yes (deployed on public internet with public IPs for one week)
deployment_justification: Section 3: "The honeypot was deployed in both low and high interaction modes on two hosts in our lab. The hosts were assigned a public IP each, under an unfiltered network." Real internet-facing one-week deployment collecting 7,587 attacks.

identifier: Safargalieva, A., Rüffer, A., & Vasilomanolakis, E. (2026). OHRA: Dynamic Multi-Protocol LLM-Based Cyber Deception. In Proceedings of NordSec 2025. Springer.
domain_justification: Abstract: "We introduce OHRA, a modular, extensible LLM-driven honeypot that supports multiple protocols (SSH, Telnet, HTTP, FTP, SMTP, SNMP, IPP) and can integrate different LLM providers." Explicitly proposes and evaluates a new multi-protocol LLM-based honeypot as primary contribution.
interaction_justification: OHRA provides full interactive LLM-generated responses for SSH, Telnet, and HTTP, with partial implementation for FTP, SMTP, IPP, and SNMP. Goes beyond scripted low-interaction but does not provide full OS access medium interaction classification.
threat_model: Automated attackers sending malware commands; sophisticated attackers capable of fingerprinting traditional static honeypots; multi-protocol attackers spanning SSH, Telnet, HTTP simultaneously.
threat_model_justification: Abstract: "We evaluate OHRA against Cowrie and a recent LLM-based honeypot using curated malware commands and a real-world Internet deployment." "OHRA is among the first honeypots to demonstrate a unified LLM-based architecture across several protocols."
irb_justification: No mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval.
consent_justification: Real-world internet deployment faces real attackers without consent. Controlled evaluation uses pre-defined attacker command sets (implicit researcher awareness but no formal consent from research participants described).
data_types_collected: Session interaction logs, attacker commands, LLM response quality scores, protocol connection statistics per protocol, returning connection patterns
data_types_justification: Table 3: "Insights from real-world deployment across seven protocols" including unique and returning connections. LLM response quality evaluated via combined realism and latency metrics.
protocols_ports: SSH (22), Telnet (23), HTTP (80), FTP (21), SMTP (25), SNMP (161), IPP (631)
protocols_justification: Protocol selection based on nmap-services file filtered by open-frequency ≥0.05 covers the most commonly internet-exposed services. Seven protocols supported.
data_sensitivity_justification: Real-world deployment logs attacker IPs and protocol interaction data. No personal user data beyond security-relevant attacker metadata. Low sensitivity.
data_sharing_justification: The paper describes an open-source modular framework supporting swappable LLM providers. Source code availability implied by the academic tradition and open-source architecture description.
jurisdiction_justification: No legal framework discussed despite real-world internet deployment and routing attacker interaction data through external LLM API providers.
containment_measures: Modular protocol services with independent logging; session memory and prompt control prevent LLM fingerprinting; "Revealing outputs" defined and monitored as a metric
containment_justification: Paper defines: "Revealing outputs are defined as honeypot responses that directly exposed the use of an LLM." Active countermeasures against fingerprinting are designed in. Each protocol service runs independently with isolated logging.
deception_justification: No ethical discussion. Deception framed entirely as a technical goal: "generate realistic, context-aware responses with less configuration effort."
researcher_responsibility_justification: No ethical guidelines, responsible disclosure, or dual-use discussion.
ethical_gaps: No IRB; no ethics section; all attacker interaction data transmitted to third-party LLM API providers same third-party data processing concern as shelLM; no GDPR compliance or data processing agreement discussion.
ethical_gaps_justification: The configurable LLM backend ("can integrate different LLM providers") means all attacker commands and session data are transmitted to whichever external LLM API the operator selects. No data processing agreement, privacy policy, or GDPR compliance discussion is included despite this constituting third-party processing of security-sensitive interaction data from real internet attackers.
relevance_to_project: Highly relevant to HoneySat ethics framework: OHRA represents current state-of-the-art in multi-protocol LLM-based honeypot design. The 7-protocol unified LLM architecture directly addresses the scalability challenge HoneySat faces when emulating multiple satellite communication protocols. Third-party LLM API dependency creates a specific ethical pillar our framework must address.
relevance_justification: OHRA's configurable multi-protocol architecture (7 protocols in one framework) and LLM-based response generation are the most technically advanced published approaches applicable to HoneySat. The absence of any governance for LLM provider selection and data processing directly motivates a dedicated "AI-honeypot governance" section in our ethics framework.
deployment_justification: Abstract: "We evaluate OHRA against Cowrie and a recent LLM-based honeypot using curated malware commands and a real-world Internet deployment." Table 3 confirms real deployment data across 7 protocols.

tool_notes: README.rst only but detailed; Master's Thesis IoT honeypot for Z-Wave protocol using SDR (RTL-SDR + HackRF One); supports passive and interactive modes.
domain_justification: Z-Wave is a wireless protocol used in smart home and IoT cyber-physical systems (smart sensors, switches, locks, thermostats). SIoTpot targets the physical wireless layer of CPS/IoT infrastructure — clearly CPS domain.
interaction_justification: README describes two modes: (1) passive monitoring (listens only) and (2) interactive mode — "transmit simulated communication to lure attackers." The interactive mode actively transmits Z-Wave frames to deceive attackers, which goes beyond passive low-interaction logging.
threat_model: Attackers targeting Z-Wave IoT infrastructure (smart home devices, industrial sensors); both passive eavesdroppers and active attackers attempting to enumerate or compromise Z-Wave networks.
threat_model_justification: README Abstract: "The motivation of this thesis was to create a device that can collect information about IoT traffic, detect potential attackers, and act as a decoy that complicates attackers to discover and hack real deployed IoT devices, such as sensors, switches."
irb_justification: Master's Thesis implementation with no mention of IRB, ethics committee, or institutional approval beyond academic thesis context.
consent_justification: No consent mechanism documented. The honeypot passively monitors and actively transmits on the Z-Wave frequency without notification to legitimate Z-Wave network participants or potential attackers.
data_types_collected: Z-Wave radio frames, network topology (HOME-ID, device IDs), communication records ("decoy records"), alert logs, attacker interaction data
data_types_justification: README describes: "records legitimate communication in order to create system of decoys" and stores records at configurable paths. Configuration file shows records_path, networks_path, logging_path, and alerts_path — four distinct data stores.
protocols_ports: Z-Wave (868.42 MHz radio frequency — not TCP/IP)
protocols_justification: README configuration: "freq = 868420000" — Z-Wave European frequency 868.42 MHz. Uses RTL-SDR dongle for reception and HackRF One for transmission. This is a radio-frequency protocol, not a TCP/IP service — unique in this dataset.
data_sensitivity_justification: Z-Wave network topology data (HOME-ID, device node IDs, communication patterns) reveals the physical layout and behaviour of real smart home/IoT devices. Recording "legitimate communication" from real Z-Wave devices captures the actual behaviour of deployed physical devices — high sensitivity in CPS context.
data_minimization_justification: No data minimization strategy discussed. The honeypot records all Z-Wave frames and stores four categories of data (records, networks, logs, alerts) without any documented filtering or minimization.
data_retention_justification: No retention policy documented. README describes a reset subcommand ("siotpot reset") that deletes all persistent data, but no policy on when or how often this should be used.
data_sharing_justification: No dataset release, public data sharing, or external submission mentioned. Source code is open-source (BSD-2-Clause); no attack dataset released.
jurisdiction_justification: No legal framework, jurisdiction analysis, or radio frequency regulatory compliance discussed despite operating on a licensed radio frequency (868.42 MHz Z-Wave band) which has regulatory requirements in different countries.
containment_measures: Partial — passive mode provides containment; interactive mode actively transmits on live Z-Wave frequency
containment_justification: README notes: "It is not recommended to use this tool as only protection of Z-Wave networks!" The interactive mode (siotpot run HOME-ID) transmits Z-Wave frames on the live radio frequency — this could interfere with real Z-Wave devices in range. No containment guidance for managing radio interference.
deception_justification: Deception is framed as a technical mechanism only: "act as a decoy that complicates attackers to discover and hack real deployed IoT devices." No ethical framing of actively transmitting deceptive signals on a live radio frequency.
researcher_responsibility_justification: No researcher responsibility statements, ethical guidelines, responsible disclosure, or dual-use discussion. The thesis README does not address the risk of radio interference to legitimate Z-Wave devices.
ethical_gaps: HIGH RISK: records legitimate Z-Wave communication from real physical devices without their owners' consent; active transmission on live radio frequency may interfere with real smart home devices; no radio frequency regulatory compliance discussion; no IRB; CPS physical-layer deception not ethically framed.
ethical_gaps_justification: The honeypot operates in the physical wireless domain — it records real Z-Wave frames from legitimate smart home devices without homeowner consent. The interactive mode actively transmits radio signals that could disrupt real Z-Wave devices (lights, locks, thermostats) in range. Radio transmission on 868.42 MHz is regulated in most jurisdictions; no compliance discussion appears in the thesis.
relevance_to_project: VERY HIGH relevance to HoneySat ethics framework: SIoTpot is the most directly analogous honeypot to HoneySat in the entire Non-Scientific Honeypots dataset — both operate at the physical wireless/radio layer, both record legitimate communication from real physical devices, and both actively transmit deceptive signals in a CPS context.
relevance_justification: SIoTpot operates on Z-Wave radio (868 MHz); HoneySat operates on satellite radio frequencies. Both share: (1) physical-layer radio deception, (2) recording legitimate CPS communication without device owner consent, (3) active signal transmission that could disrupt real infrastructure, (4) complete absence of ethical governance. SIoTpot is the single most compelling non-ICS case study for the CPS ethics pillar of our framework.
deployment: Not documented; designed for deployment in real Z-Wave network environments
deployment_justification: README describes deployment within a real Z-Wave network (requires real HOME-ID, uses real RTL-SDR and HackRF hardware). Testing was done using a single transmitter on a notebook — physical deployment facing real Z-Wave signals.
